chunks.about: USCIS guidance to its officers: how the agency applies the regulations

chunks.citation: Volume 8, Part C, Chapter 4 - Termination and Revocation
chunks.heading: Chapter 4 - Termination and Revocation
chunks.text:
In instances where the civil surgeon may be involved in fraud, USCIS Fraud Detection and National Security Directorate (FDNS) should be notified per the standard fraud referral operating procedures and the civil surgeon’s record should be annotated to reflect that suspected fraud played a factor in initiating revocation. Depending on the nature and severity of the allegations, it may also be necessary to consult with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) to obtain expert medical advice.
An officer may refer a proposed revocation of civil surgeon designation to USCIS counsel for review. When referring a case to USCIS counsel, the officer should include the reasons for the intended revocation and a copy of the supporting evidence.
Once the decision has been made to initiate the revocation, the officer must serve the physician with a notice of intent to revoke by Certified Mail/Return Receipt Requested or other method that provides proof of delivery. The notice must clearly state the exact grounds for the intended revocation and include copies of any relevant evidence. [2] The officer must give the physician 30 days from the date of the notice to respond with countervailing evidence. The physician may be represented by private counsel at his or her own expense. [3]
The authority to designate civil surgeons does not give USCIS authority to regulate the practice of medicine. For this reason, the process for revoking designation as a civil surgeon is not the proper forum for adjudicating complaints against a physician concerning malpractice, breach of medical ethics, or other improper conduct. If USCIS receives a complaint of this kind, USCIS should advise the complainant to make the complaint with the proper medical licensing authority for the State or territory in which the physician practices.
Once the period for the physician’s response to the notice of intent to revoke has expired, USCIS reviews the record and decide whether to revoke the physician’s designation as a civil surgeon. Any response from the physician is included in the record of proceeding. USCIS must notify the physician in writing of the decision.
There is no administrative appeal from a decision to revoke a physician’s designation as a civil surgeon. The physician may, however, file a motion to reopen or reconsider. [4] A decision revoking a physician’s designation as a civil surgeon must notify the physician of the right to file a timely motion to reopen or reconsider.
chunks.about: USCIS guidance to its officers: how the agency applies the regulations

chunks.citation: Volume 8, Part C, Chapter 4 - Termination and Revocation
chunks.heading: Chapter 4 - Termination and Revocation
chunks.text:
Similarly, USCIS may reopen and reconsider a decision on its own motion. A physician whose civil surgeon designation is revoked is not precluded from reapplying for civil surgeon designation, but the ground(s) upon which revocation is based should be considered as part of the adjudication of a subsequent application for civil surgeon designation. A physician, however, whose prior civil surgeon designation was revoked based on confirmed involvement in an immigration benefits fraud scheme will be denied civil surgeon designation upon reapplication.
If USCIS revokes a physician’s designation as a civil surgeon, the public civil surgeon list should be updated immediately to remove the civil surgeon’s information. [5]
If an officer reviewing Form I-693 has a concern about the sufficiency of an immigration medical examination performed by a physician who was designated at the time of the medical exam but subsequently had his or her designation revoked, the officer may reorder the medical exam to be performed by a civil surgeon to address the concern. [6]
[^ 1] For more information on where to send a request to terminate one’s designation, visit the USCIS website .
[^ 2] USCIS may redact certain sensitive or identifying information.
[^ 3] Notice of Entry of Appearance as Attorney or Accredited Representative ( Form G-28 ) must also be filed in this case.
[^ 4] As permitted in 8 CFR 103.5 . To file a motion to reopen or reconsider, a physician should file a Notice of Appeal or Motion ( Form I-290B ), with fee. Forms and fee information can be found at uscis.gov .
[^ 5] As specified in Chapter 5, Civil Surgeon List [ 8 USCIS-PM C.5 ].
[^ 6] In general, an officer may order or reorder an immigration medical examination, in part or in whole, at any time if he or she has concerns regarding an applicant’s inadmissibility on health-related grounds. See Volume 8, Admissibility, Part B, Health-Related Grounds of Inadmissibility [ 8 USCIS-PM B ].
chunks.about: USCIS guidance to its officers: how the agency applies the regulations

chunks.citation: Volume 8, Part C, Chapter 5 - Civil Surgeon List
chunks.heading: Chapter 5 - Civil Surgeon List
chunks.text:
USCIS maintains a nationwide list of civil surgeons available to the public. Applicants may search the list for civil surgeons designated in their area at USCIS.gov (via the Civil Surgeon Locator) or through the USCIS Contact Center’s toll-free number at 1-800-375-5283.
Physicians on the civil surgeon list are generally current in their designation as civil surgeons. Since the list is updated weekly, it is advisable for the applicants to check that a physician is still on the civil surgeon list as close as possible to the date of the immigration medical exam appointment. If uncertain, applicants should also confirm with their doctors regarding their civil surgeon status prior to the immigration medical examination.
A civil surgeon should inform USCIS of any change that is relevant to the civil surgeon designation within 15 days of the change. [1]
If an officer at a USCIS field or district office receives a request to update the civil surgeon list, he or she should forward the request to the National Benefits Center (NBC) for review.
USCIS reviews all requests from civil surgeons to update contact information or to terminate the civil surgeon designation. USCIS also updates the civil surgeon list accordingly, as well as removes civil surgeons whose designations have been suspended or revoked.
If a civil surgeon’s request to update contact information involves a move to a new state, then evidence of medical licensure in the new state [2] must accompany the request before the officer may approve it. If this evidence is missing, the officer may request this information through the issuance of a Request for Evidence (RFE).
If a civil surgeon requests to be removed from the civil surgeon list or if USCIS determines designation should be suspended or revoked, the officer should annotate the date and reason for removal. Records of former civil surgeons should be retained internally; the information may be relevant, for instance, to the adjudication of a medical examination the civil surgeon completed before he or she was removed from the civil surgeon list or if the physician re-applies for civil surgeon designation in the future.
USCIS ensures the civil surgeon list is updated in a timely manner to reflect any changes in a civil surgeon’s contact information or designation status. In addition, USCIS performs a review of the civil surgeon list on a bi-annual basis, at a minimum, to ensure that all publicly available civil surgeon information is current and accurate.

USCIS should follow regular revocation procedures.

chunks.citation: Volume 8, Part D, Chapter 10 - Controlled Substance Traffickers
chunks.heading: Chapter 10 - Controlled Substance Traffickers
chunks.text:
Section 212(a)(2)(C) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) bars the admission of aliens involved in illicit trafficking of a controlled substance or certain designated chemicals. Aliens inadmissible under this ground include:
Keeping the United States safe from the trafficking of controlled substances has long been a priority of the United States [5] since even before the consolidation of immigration laws in the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) in 1952. [6] Early laws restricting the import, manufacture, sale, and dealing in certain drugs imposed immigration consequences for violations. [7]
The INA established section 212(a)(23), [8] that excluded aliens from the United States who were convicted of certain drug offenses, as well as aliens who were convicted of a violation of any law or regulation relating to the illicit trafficking of certain narcotic drugs or any alien who consular or immigration officers “know or have reason to believe is or has been an illicit trafficker” in those drugs.
Congress enacted the Controlled Substances Act (CSA) in 1970 to create a unified legal framework to regulate certain drugs and other substances that are deemed to pose a risk of abuse and dependence, [9] and in 1986, Congress amended INA 212(a)(23) by replacing the list of drug-related conduct and substances with a general reference to any law or regulation of a State, the United States, or a foreign country relating to a controlled substance as defined in section 102 of the CSA. [10]
In 1987, Congress amended INA 212(a)(23) and established a separate provision to exclude aliens who immigration or consular officers know or have reason to believe are or have been illicit traffickers in a controlled substance, as defined in section 102 of the CSA, from entering the United States. [11] The amendments also excluded aliens who immigration or consular officers know or have reason to believe are or have knowingly assisted, abetted, conspired, or colluded with others in the illicit trafficking of controlled substances. [12]
In 1996, Congress enacted the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act (IIRIRA), which redesignated provisions in INA 212(a) from grounds of exclusion to inadmissibility and added, removed, and modified several grounds. [13] The ground of inadmissibility for controlled substance traffickers moved to INA 212(a)(2)(C) without any changes to the inadmissibility provisions. In 1999, Congress expanded INA 212(a)(2)(C) to make certain family members who have obtained any financial or other benefit from the illicit activity of an alien inadmissible under that provision in certain circumstances. [14]
chunks.about: USCIS guidance to its officers: how the agency applies the regulations

chunks.citation: Volume 8, Part D, Chapter 10 - Controlled Substance Traffickers
chunks.heading: Chapter 10 - Controlled Substance Traffickers
chunks.text:
An alien is inadmissible under INA 212(a)(2)(C) if he or she is or has been an illicit trafficker in any controlled substance or in any listed chemical as defined in 21 U.S.C. 802 ; is or has been or has endeavored to be a knowing aider, abettor, assister, conspirator, or colluder with others in the illicit trafficking of any such controlled or listed substance or chemical; or is the spouse, son, or daughter of such an alien where the spouse, son, or daughter has, within the previous 5 years, obtained any financial or other benefit from the illicit activity and knew or reasonably should have known that the financial or other benefit was the product of such illicit activity. [15]
A conviction is not required to find an alien inadmissible as a controlled substance trafficker under INA 212(a)(2)(C). [16] The officer must know, or have a reason to believe, that the alien was involved in illicit trafficking of a controlled substance or listed chemical. [17]
21 U.S.C. 802 defines the term “controlled substance” as "a drug or other substance, or immediate precursor, included in schedule I, II, III, IV, or V of part B of this subchapter." [18] 21 U.S.C. 802 defines the term “listed chemical” as “any list I chemical or any list II chemical.” [19] For determinations of inadmissibility, it is generally irrelevant under which specific schedule, list, or classification the “controlled substance” or “listed chemical” is specifically identified in 21 U.S.C. 802.
If the substance involved is not listed in 21 U.S.C. 802 as either a controlled substance or listed chemical, then the alien is not inadmissible under INA 212(a)(2)(C) . [20] Officers must determine if the substance involved was listed in 21 U.S.C. 802 at the time of the trafficking. If the substance or chemical involved was not listed at the time that the alien or their spouse or parent was trafficking the substance or chemical, then the alien is not inadmissible (even if the substance or chemical has subsequently been listed). [21] If the substance or chemical was listed at the time of the trafficking, but not listed at the time of the inadmissibility determination, the alien may be inadmissible.
The phrase “illicit trafficking” is not defined in the INA, but INA 212(a)(2)(C) applies to a broad range of activities, including, but not limited to:
Officers may also consider activities involving the sale, transfer, transportation, production, cultivation or manufacture of a controlled substance, regardless of the alien’s level of involvement, as this ground of inadmissibility applies given the inclusion of these types of activities in federal criminal laws related to drug trafficking. [27]
chunks.about: USCIS guidance to its officers: how the agency applies the regulations

chunks.citation: Volume 8, Part D, Chapter 10 - Controlled Substance Traffickers
chunks.heading: Chapter 10 - Controlled Substance Traffickers
chunks.text:
The term “illicit trafficker” does not require that an alien has been continuously engaged in such activity. [28] Illicit trafficking includes aliens, who on a single occasion, have dealt in controlled substances or listed chemicals. [29] Accordingly, an alien’s involvement as an illicit trafficker may consist of a single act in the past or present.
An alien who is the spouse, son, or daughter of an alien who is inadmissible as an illicit trafficker of any controlled substance is inadmissible if the spouse, son, or daughter:
The statute requires that the financial or other benefit has been obtained within the previous 5 years for the beneficiary of trafficking to be inadmissible under INA 212(a)(2)(C)(ii) . However, even if the financial or other benefit was not obtained by the spouse, son, or daughter within the previous 5 years, when the spouse, son, or daughter applies for a discretionary immigration benefit, the officer may consider the financial or other benefit obtained as the product of the illicit activity as a negative factor when determining if a favorable exercise of discretion is warranted.
The officer also considers how long ago and the length of time the financial or other benefit that was knowingly (or that the alien reasonably should have known was) received by the spouse, son, or daughter, as well as the amount received when determining the weight to attribute to this negative factor in a case-by-case discretionary analysis. [31]
An alien who is the spouse, son, or daughter of an inadmissible alien is also inadmissible as a controlled substance trafficker even if the alien’s spouse or parent was not previously found inadmissible under INA 212(a)(2)(C)(i) .
In cases in which the alien’s spouse or parent was not previously found inadmissible as a controlled substance trafficker, an officer must assess whether the spouse or parent would be found inadmissible for controlled substance trafficking if that spouse or parent were to apply for an immigration benefit.
An alien who meets the definition of spouse can be found inadmissible as the beneficiary of controlled substance trafficking if the spouse is currently married to the alien who is inadmissible as a controlled substance trafficker at the time the inadmissibility determination is made. If the marriage has been terminated due to divorce or death of the alien inadmissible as a controlled substance trafficker, the former spouse may not be found inadmissible under INA 212(a)(2)(C)(ii) .
chunks.about: USCIS guidance to its officers: how the agency applies the regulations

chunks.citation: Volume 8, Part D, Chapter 10 - Controlled Substance Traffickers
chunks.heading: Chapter 10 - Controlled Substance Traffickers
chunks.text:
However, when the former spouse is applying for a discretionary benefit, [32] if the former spouse obtained any financial or other benefit from the illicit activity of his or her former spouse and knew or reasonably should have known that the benefit was the product of such illicit activity, then the officer may consider the financial or other benefit obtained as the product of the illicit activity as a negative factor when determining if a favorable exercise of discretion is warranted.
The officer should evaluate how long ago and the length of time the financial or other benefit that was knowingly (or that the alien reasonably should have known was) received, as well as the amount of benefit received, along with any extenuating circumstances when determining the weight to attribute to this negative factor in a case-by-case discretionary analysis. [33]
An alien who is a son or daughter of an alien inadmissible as a controlled substance trafficker remains the son or daughter of such an alien who is inadmissible under INA 212(a)(2)(C)(i) even after the death of that alien. Additionally, a stepparent-stepchild relationship may continue to exist for immigration purposes after the death of the natural parent or after the divorce of the stepparent and natural parent if there is an ongoing relationship between the stepparent and stepchild. [34]
A determination of inadmissibility for being a controlled substance trafficker only requires an officer to know or have a “reason to believe” that:
The reason to believe standard can be established through the existence of a conviction. [35] Indeed, a conviction for controlled substance trafficking is prima facie evidence [36] that the alien is inadmissible under INA 212(a)(2)(C)(i) .
However, no conviction is required to find an alien inadmissible as a controlled substance trafficker or as the spouse, son, or daughter of an alien inadmissible as a controlled substance trafficker. [37] If the officer has reason to believe the alien is or has been involved in the controlled substance trafficking, or is the spouse, son, or daughter of such an alien who obtained any financial or other benefit of the illicit activity in the previous 5 years and knew or reasonably should have known that the financial or other benefit was the product of such illicit activity, then the officer can find the alien inadmissible under INA 212(a)(2)(C)(i) or (ii), as applicable. [38]
Even if the alien is arrested for, but not ultimately charged with, an illicit trafficking offense, or if a criminal complaint has been dismissed, an alien may still be inadmissible. An officer may also consider the facts of an underlying offense, even if the conviction was ultimately vacated or expunged, when determining whether an alien is inadmissible under this ground.

chunks.citation: Volume 8, Part D, Chapter 10 - Controlled Substance Traffickers
chunks.heading: Chapter 10 - Controlled Substance Traffickers
chunks.text:
A formal admission or statement, sworn testimony, a record of arrest, or reliable and corroborative reports may be sufficient evidence for an officer to have a reason to believe that an alien is inadmissible under INA 212(a)(2)(C). At the same time, mere suspicion is not sufficient to find an alien inadmissible under the reason to believe standard.
There must exist a probability, supported by evidence, that the alien is or has been involved in or benefited from controlled substance trafficking. A determination that an alien is inadmissible as a controlled substance trafficker should be supported by reasonable, substantial, and probative evidence. [39]
There are no statutory exceptions under INA 212(a)(2)(C) .
For certain immigration benefits, aliens are not subject to the inadmissibility ground under INA 212(a)(2)(C) . Some immigrant categories listed on the Application to Register Permanent Residence or Adjust Status ( Form I-485 ) to register or obtain documentation of their lawful permanent resident (LPR) status are not subject to an inadmissibility determination. These categories of LPRs, including individuals born in the United States under diplomatic status and American Indians born in Canada, are therefore exempt from this inadmissibility ground. [40]
Other immigration benefits and immigrant categories that are not subject to this ground include:
While there is no waiver available for this ground of inadmissibility within INA 212 , Congress has established a few category-specific waivers in other sections of law. [48]
A waiver is distinct from the statutory exemptions. The exemptions are automatic, based on the immigration benefit sought or the immigrant category. The alien does not need to formally request an exemption and there are no other eligibility criteria. In contrast, an alien must formally request a waiver from USCIS and demonstrate that he or she meets all of the eligibility requirements for that waiver and merits a favorable exercise of discretion. Examples of categories or immigration benefits where a waiver is available for this ground include, but are not limited to:
This ground of inadmissibility applies to any alien seeking an immigration benefit for which admissibility is required. This includes, but is not limited to, adjustment of status to that of an LPR, an alien who is applying for an immigrant visa with the U.S. Department of State (DOS) at a U.S. embassy or consulate outside of the United States, or an alien applying for admission as an immigrant at a U.S. port of entry. [53]
The burden of proof to establish admissibility when seeking an immigration benefit is always on the alien. [54] The burden never shifts to the U.S. government at any time during adjudication. [55]

chunks.citation: Volume 8, Part D, Chapter 10 - Controlled Substance Traffickers

chunks.text:
The burden of proof to establish admissibility when seeking an immigration benefit is always on the alien. [54] The burden never shifts to the U.S. government at any time during adjudication. [55]
If there is evidence in the record that would permit a reasonable person to conclude that the alien is inadmissible under this ground, the officer should find that the alien has not successfully met the burden of proof.
An alien who fails to meet the burden of proof is inadmissible under INA 212(a)(2)(C) unless the alien is able to show clearly and beyond doubt [56] that he or she:
A finding of inadmissibility under INA 212(a)(2)(C) must be based on evidence, such as criminal convictions, arrest records, security and systems checks, oral testimony, written testimony, or any other documentation containing information about the alien’s involvement in controlled substance trafficking or about how the alien derived benefits from the controlled substance trafficking.
USCIS considers responses on applications and petitions as evidence when determining if an alien is inadmissible under INA 212(a)(2)(C). [57] Some USCIS forms, including Form I-485 , require aliens to indicate if they have ever trafficked in or benefited from, or knowingly aided, assisted, conspired or colluded in the illegal trafficking of any controlled substances, such as chemicals, illegal drugs, or narcotics. Form I-485 also requires aliens to indicate if, within the last 5 years, they obtained from a spouse or parent any financial or other benefit from illicit trafficking of a controlled substance or listed substance or chemical.
If an alien misrepresents information regarding illicit trafficking of a controlled substance or listed substance or chemical or obtaining financial or other benefits from illicit trafficking when answering questions on Form I-485, the alien could also be found inadmissible under INA 212(a)(6)(C)(i) . [58]
In general, USCIS is required to provide sufficient notice when derogatory information is uncovered during the course of the adjudication that is not known to the alien and USCIS intends to deny the benefit request on the basis of that derogatory information. [59] If the alien is unaware of the derogatory information and its impact on eligibility, USCIS must provide the alien an opportunity to rebut that information. [60]

chunks.citation: Volume 8, Part D, Chapter 14 - Significant Traffickers in Persons
chunks.heading: Chapter 14 - Significant Traffickers in Persons
chunks.text:
Section 212(a)(2)(H) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) is designed to protect the United States and its people from human trafficking by rendering any alien involved in human trafficking inside or outside the United States inadmissible. Under INA 212(a)(2)(H)(i) , the following aliens are inadmissible:
Additionally, the following aliens are inadmissible under INA 212(a)(2)(H)(ii) :
In 2000, Congress passed the Victims of Trafficking and Violence Protection Act of 2000 (TVPA) (PDF) , adding INA 212(a)(2)(H) to the inadmissibility grounds. [4] This provision made aliens who have been involved in or benefited from severe forms of trafficking in persons inadmissible to the United States. The TVPA was intended to help combat trafficking in persons, especially into the sex trade, slavery, and involuntary servitude in the United States and countries around the world through prevention, through prosecution and enforcement against traffickers, and through protection and assistance to victims of trafficking. [5]
Congress did not provide any waivers of this inadmissibility ground in INA 212 . However, an exception was included [6] for any son or daughter of an alien inadmissible under INA 212(a)(2)(H)(ii), provided the son or daughter was a child [7] at the time he or she obtained any financial or other benefit from his or her alien parent’s involvement in the illicit activity. Additionally, certain categories of nonimmigrants and immigrants may be exempt or have a waiver of inadmissibility available under other sections of law. [8]
This ground of inadmissibility references a number of definitions under 22 U.S.C. 7102 , which are critical to making human trafficking inadmissibility determinations.
“Severe forms of trafficking in persons,” as defined in 22 U.S.C. 7102(11) , means:
“Sex trafficking,” as defined in 22 U.S.C. 7102(12) , means the recruitment, harboring, transportation, provision, obtaining, patronizing, or soliciting of a person for the purpose of a commercial sex act.
“Coercion,” as defined in 22 U.S.C. 7102(3) , means:
"Involuntary servitude," as defined in 22 U.S.C. 7102(8) , includes a condition of servitude induced by means of:
"Debt bondage," as defined in 22 U.S.C. 7102(7) , means the status or condition of a debtor arising from a pledge by the debtor of his or her personal services or of those of a person under his or her control as a security for debt, if the value of those services as reasonably assessed is not applied toward the liquidation of the debt or the length and nature of those services are not respectively limited and defined.

chunks.citation: Volume 8, Part D, Chapter 14 - Significant Traffickers in Persons
chunks.heading: Chapter 14 - Significant Traffickers in Persons
chunks.text:
The initial language of INA 212(a)(2)(H)(i) provided that any alien who is listed and identified as a significant trafficker in persons in a report to Congress is inadmissible. [15] The referenced report included “any foreign person” [16] who played a significant role or materially assisted in a severe form of trafficking in persons, directly or indirectly in the United States. [17]
In 2008, Congress amended INA 212(a)(2)(H)(i) to replace the reference to any alien listed as a significant trafficker in persons with any alien “who commits or conspires to commit human trafficking offenses in the United States or outside the United States.” [18] This broadened the scope of aliens who may be found inadmissible as significant traffickers in persons by not limiting inadmissibility to only those “foreign persons” identified and reported to Congress.
The spouse, son, or daughter of an alien who is inadmissible as a significant trafficker in persons is inadmissible if the spouse, son, or daughter:
The statute requires that the financial or other benefit has been obtained within the previous 5 years for the beneficiary of trafficking to be inadmissible under INA 212(a)(2)(H)(ii) . However, when the spouse, son, or daughter of the alien inadmissible under INA 212(a)(2)(H)(i) applies for a discretionary immigration benefit, an officer may still consider any financial or other benefit that was knowingly (or that the alien reasonably should have known was) obtained as the product of the illicit activity at any time as a negative factor when determining if a favorable exercise of discretion is warranted.
The officer also considers how long ago and the length of time the benefit was that was knowingly (or that the alien reasonably should have known was) received, as well as the amount received when determining the weight to attribute to this negative factor in a case-by-case discretionary analysis. [21]
A spouse, son, or daughter can be found inadmissible as the beneficiary of trafficking even if his or her inadmissible spouse or parent had not previously been found inadmissible under INA 212(a)(2)(H)(i) by an immigration judge, DHS, or DOS.
In cases involving the spouse, son, or daughter of an inadmissible spouse or parent, an officer must assess that his or her spouse or parent would be found inadmissible under INA 212(a)(2)(H)(i) if his or her spouse or parent were to apply for an immigration benefit, and then determine if the spouse, son, or daughter is inadmissible as the beneficiary of trafficking.

chunks.citation: Volume 8, Part D, Chapter 14 - Significant Traffickers in Persons
chunks.heading: Chapter 14 - Significant Traffickers in Persons
chunks.text:
An alien who meets the definition of spouse can be found inadmissible as the beneficiary of trafficking if the spouse is currently married to the alien who is inadmissible under INA 212(a)(2)(H)(i) . If the marriage has been terminated due to divorce or death of the inadmissible spouse, then the former spouse may not be found inadmissible as the beneficiary of trafficking.
An officer may also, as part of a discretionary determination, consider the fact that an alien benefited from the illicit activity of a former spouse if at any time he or she knew or reasonably should have known that the benefit was the product of such illicit activity, when he or she applies for a discretionary immigration benefit. [22] The officer may consider this as a negative factor when determining if a favorable exercise of discretion is warranted. The officer should evaluate how long ago and the length of time the benefit was knowingly received and the amount received, along with any extenuating circumstances when determining the weight to attribute to this negative factor in a case-by-case discretionary analysis. [23]
The son or daughter of an alien inadmissible under INA 212(a)(2)(H)(i) remains the son or daughter of that inadmissible parent even after the death of the parent. Additionally, a step-relationship may continue to exist for immigration purposes after the death of the natural parent or after the divorce of the stepparent and natural parent if there is an ongoing relationship between the stepparent and stepchild. [24]
A determination of inadmissibility for being a knowing aider, abettor, assister, conspirator, or colluder of a significant trafficker in persons or for finding an alien to be the beneficiary of severe forms of trafficking in persons only requires a “reason to believe.” [25] “Reason to believe" is substantially lower than what would be required for a conviction in a court of law.
At the same time, suspicion is not sufficient to find an alien inadmissible under the reason to believe standard. There must be reasonable, substantial, and probative evidence to support the belief that the alien either is involved or has been involved with severe forms of trafficking in persons or is benefitting from or has benefitted from trafficking. [26]

chunks.citation: Volume 8, Part D, Chapter 14 - Significant Traffickers in Persons
chunks.heading: Chapter 14 - Significant Traffickers in Persons
chunks.text:
If the alien has been convicted of aiding, abetting, assisting, conspiring, or colluding with a trafficker to commit a severe form of trafficking in persons offense, the conviction is evidence that the alien is inadmissible under INA 212(a)(2)(H)(i) . However, a conviction is not required for an alien to be inadmissible. For example, an alien could be found inadmissible under INA 212(a)(2)(H)(i) even though criminal charges have been dismissed, or even if an alien has never been arrested. USCIS may also have reason to believe an alien is a knowing aider, abettor, assister, conspirator, or colluder of a trafficker in severe forms of trafficking in persons based on the alien’s admission, a record of arrests with an unexplained failure to prosecute by the local government, or reliable and corroborative reports.
Similarly, an alien’s spouse or parent is not required to be convicted of a human trafficking or severe form of trafficking in persons offense for an alien to be inadmissible as a beneficiary of trafficking. Additionally, an alien is not required to be convicted of benefiting financially or in any other way from human trafficking or severe forms of trafficking in persons to be inadmissible. [27]
A son or daughter who was a child [28] at the time he or she received the benefits of the illicit activity of their parent is not inadmissible under INA 212(a)(2)(H)(ii) . [29] There is no exception in the statute applicable to current spouses who benefited from the illicit activity of their spouse.
For certain immigration benefits, aliens are not subject to the inadmissibility ground under INA 212(a)(2)(H) . Some immigrant categories listed on the Application to Register Permanent Residence or Adjust Status ( Form I-485 ) to register or obtain documentation of their lawful permanent resident (LPR) status are not subject to an inadmissibility determination. These categories of LPRs, including individuals born in the United States under diplomatic status and American Indians born in Canada, are therefore exempt from this inadmissibility ground. [30]
Victims of qualifying criminal activity (U nonimmigrants) applying for adjustment of status under INA 245(m) are also exempt from the significant trafficking in persons inadmissibility, because the ground does not apply to their immigrant category. [31]
Additionally, some nonimmigrant categories are not subject to INA 212(a)(2)(H) , including:
While there is no immigrant waiver available for this ground of inadmissibility within INA 212 , Congress has established a few category-specific waivers in other sections of law. [33]

Additionally, some nonimmigrant categories are not subject to INA 212(a)(2)(H) , including:
While there is no immigrant waiver available for this ground of inadmissibility within INA 212 , Congress has established a few category-specific waivers in other sections of law. [33]
A waiver is distinct from the statutory exemptions. The exemptions are automatic, based on the immigration benefit sought or the immigrant category. The alien does not need to make a formal request for an exemption and there are no other eligibility criteria. In contrast, an alien must formally request a waiver from USCIS and demonstrate that he or she meets all the eligibility requirements for that waiver and merits a favorable exercise of discretion. Examples of immigrant categories where a waiver is available for this ground include aliens applying for adjustment to lawful permanent residence as:
Aliens may also apply for a waiver of this inadmissibility when applying for certain other immigration benefits, including, but not limited to, aliens seeking:
INA 212(d)(3)(A) provides for a discretionary waiver of inadmissibility under INA 212(a)(2)(H) for an alien applying for admission to the United States as a nonimmigrant.
This ground of inadmissibility applies to any alien seeking a benefit for which admissibility is required. This includes, but is not limited to, any alien seeking admission to the United States at a U.S. port of entry, any alien seeking a nonimmigrant or immigrant visa with DOS at a U.S. embassy or consulate outside of the United States, or any alien seeking adjustment of status. [44]
The burden of proof to establish admissibility when seeking an immigration benefit is always on the alien. [45] The burden never shifts to USCIS at any time during adjudication. [46]
If there is evidence in the record that would permit a reasonable person to conclude that the alien is inadmissible under INA 212(a)(2)(H)(i), the officer should find that the alien is inadmissible unless the alien is able to show clearly and beyond doubt [47] that he or she:
If there is evidence in the record that would permit a reasonable person to conclude that the alien is inadmissible under INA 212(a)(2)(H)(ii), the officer should find that the alien is inadmissible unless the alien is able to show clearly and beyond doubt [48] that he or she:
A finding of inadmissibility under INA 212(a)(2)(H) must be based on evidence, such as convictions, arrest records, systems and security checks, oral testimony, written testimony, or any other documentation containing information about the alien’s involvement in the severe trafficking in persons.
An alien’s conviction for human trafficking offenses is prima facie evidence [49] that the alien is inadmissible under INA 212(a)(2)(H)(i).

chunks.citation: Volume 8, Part D, Chapter 14 - Significant Traffickers in Persons
chunks.heading: Chapter 14 - Significant Traffickers in Persons
chunks.text:
An alien’s conviction for human trafficking offenses is prima facie evidence [49] that the alien is inadmissible under INA 212(a)(2)(H)(i).
USCIS considers responses on applications and petitions as evidence when determining if an alien is inadmissible under INA 212(a)(2)(H) . [50] Some USCIS forms, including Form I-485 , require aliens to indicate if they have ever been involved in the trafficking of another person, or if they have benefited from a spouse or parent’s involvement in the trafficking of another person.
If an alien misrepresents information regarding severe trafficking in persons when answering questions on Form I-485, the alien could also be found inadmissible under INA 212(a)(6)(C)(i) . [51]
In general, USCIS is required to provide sufficient notice when derogatory information is uncovered during the course of the adjudication that is not known to the alien and USCIS intends to deny the benefit request on the basis of that derogatory information. [52] If the alien is unaware of the derogatory information and its impact on eligibility, USCIS must provide the alien an opportunity to rebut that information. [53]
The tables below map out the process for making significant trafficking in persons admissibility determinations by class of alien described in INA 212(a)(2)(H) .
The following table provides officers with an overview of how to determine whether an alien is inadmissible for committing or conspiring to commit human trafficking offenses. [54]
The officer may issue a Request for Evidence (RFE) or Notice of Intent to Deny (NOID) to the alien to provide him or her an opportunity to request a waiver, unless already requested.
If the waiver is approved, the officer should continue with the adjudication of the application.
An officer only needs to find the alien has committed or conspired to commit human trafficking offenses inside or outside of the United States. A conviction is not required for an alien to be inadmissible under this ground. However, if the alien was convicted of a human trafficking offense, the conviction is evidence that the alien is inadmissible under INA 212(a)(2)(H)(i) .
The following table provides officers with an overview of how to determine whether an alien is inadmissible as an aider, abettor, assister, conspirator, or colluder of traffickers in severe forms of trafficking in persons. [58]

chunks.citation: Volume 8, Part D, Chapter 15 - Money Laundering
chunks.heading: Chapter 15 - Money Laundering
chunks.text:
Section 212(a)(2)(I) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) makes any alien involved in money laundering inadmissible to the United States.
Under INA 212(a)(2)(I) , the following are inadmissible to the United States:
Generally, money laundering facilitates a broad range of serious underlying criminal offenses and ultimately threatens the integrity of the financial system because it involves financial transactions in which criminals, including terrorist organizations, attempt to disguise the proceeds, sources, or nature of their illicit activities.
The money laundering ground of inadmissibility was added to the INA in the Uniting and Strengthening America by Providing Appropriate Tools Required to Intercept and Obstruct Terrorism Act of 2001 (USA PATRIOT Act), which was passed, in part, by Congress to strengthen measures to prevent the use of U.S. financial systems for personal gain by foreign officials. [3]
There are no waivers or exceptions included in the statutory language of INA 212 . However, certain categories of nonimmigrants and immigrants are exempt from this ground of inadmissibility or have a waiver of inadmissibility available to them under other sections of law. [4]
The money laundering ground of inadmissibility references a number of definitions in 18 U.S.C. 1956 and 18 U.S.C. 1957 that are critical to making money laundering inadmissibility determinations.
In general, money laundering refers to financial transactions in which criminals attempt to disguise the proceeds, sources, or nature of their illicit activities. For purposes of inadmissibility determinations under INA 212(a)(2)(I) , the statute specifies that money laundering means an offense described in 18 U.S.C. 1956 or 18 U.S.C. 1957 .
Conduct criminalized by these two federal laws includes the following: [5]
“Monetary instruments,” as defined in 18 U.S.C. 1956(c)(5) , means:
“Monetary transactions,” as defined in 18 U.S.C. 1957(f)(1) , means the deposit, withdrawal, transfer, or exchange, in or affecting interstate or foreign commerce, of funds or a monetary instrument [11] by, through, or to a financial institution, [12] including any transaction that would be a financial transaction. [13]
A “financial transaction,” as defined in 18 U.S.C. 1956(c)(4) , means a transaction:

A “financial transaction,” as defined in 18 U.S.C. 1956(c)(4) , means a transaction:
The federal money laundering statutes are complex, but they include four basic components. To determine whether an alien is inadmissible for having engaged in money laundering, an officer’s findings should include that:
An officer only needs to know or have reason to believe [16] an alien has engaged, is engaging, or seeks to enter the United States to engage in an offense described in 18 U.S.C. 1956 or 18 U.S.C. 1957 (money laundering offenses), or has knowingly aided, abetted, assisted, conspired, or colluded with others in such an offense. A conviction is not required; officers may rely on any reasonable, substantial, and probative evidence in the record. [17] .
A determination of inadmissibility for money laundering under INA 212(a)(2)(I) only requires the officer to have a “reason to believe.” Reason to believe is substantially lower than what would be required for a conviction in a court of law. At the same time, a suspicion is not sufficient to find an alien inadmissible under the reason to believe standard. There must be reasonable, substantial, and probative evidence to support the belief that the alien is engaged in money laundering. [18]
For example, an alien could be found inadmissible even though criminal charges have been dismissed, or even if an alien has never been arrested. USCIS may also have reason to believe the alien has engaged in or is engaged in money laundering based on an alien’s admission, a record of arrests with failure to prosecute by the government, or reliable and corroborative reports.
If an alien is convicted of a money laundering offense as defined in 18 U.S.C. 1956 or 18 U.S.C. 1957 , the conviction is evidence that the alien is inadmissible under INA 212(a)(2)(I) . A conviction is not required for an officer to find the alien inadmissible for money laundering, but the officer should be able to articulate specific facts relevant to a specific federal criminal money laundering statute as defined in 18 U.S.C. 1956 or 18 U.S.C. 1957 . Mere suspicion is not sufficient to find an alien inadmissible for money laundering.
There are no statutory exceptions under the money laundering ground of inadmissibility at INA 212(a)(2)(I) .

chunks.text:
There are no statutory exceptions under the money laundering ground of inadmissibility at INA 212(a)(2)(I) .
For certain immigrant benefits, aliens are not subject to the inadmissibility ground under INA 212(a)(2)(I). Some immigrant categories may be listed on the Application to Register Permanent Residence or Adjust Status ( Form I-485 ) to register or obtain documentation of their lawful permanent resident (LPR) status, but are not subject to an inadmissibility determination. These categories of LPRs, including individuals born in the United States under diplomatic status and American Indians born in Canada, are therefore exempt from this inadmissibility ground. [19]
Victims of qualifying criminal activity (U nonimmigrants) applying for adjustment of status under INA 245(m) are also exempt from the money laundering ground of inadmissibility, because the ground does not apply to their immigrant category. [20]
Additionally, some nonimmigrant categories are not subject to INA 212(a)(2)(I) , including:
Although there is no waiver of inadmissibility for this ground in INA 212 for immigrants, Congress has established a few category-specific waivers in other sections of law. [22]
A waiver is distinct from the statutory exemptions. The exemptions are automatic, based on the immigration benefit sought or the immigrant category. The alien does not need to formally request an exemption and there are no other eligibility criteria. In contrast, an alien must formally request a waiver from USCIS and demonstrate that he or she meets all of the eligibility requirements for that waiver and merits a favorable exercise of discretion. Examples of immigrant categories where a waiver is available for this ground include aliens applying for adjustment to lawful permanent residence as:
Aliens may also apply for a waiver of this inadmissibility when applying for certain other immigration benefits, including, but not limited to, aliens seeking:
INA 212(d)(3)(A) provides for a discretionary waiver of inadmissibility under INA 212(a)(2)(I) for an alien applying for admission to the United States as a nonimmigrant.
This ground of inadmissibility applies to any alien seeking a benefit for which admissibility is required, such as an alien inside the United States applying for adjustment of status to that of an LPR, [33] an alien applying for an immigrant or nonimmigrant visa with the U.S. Department of State (DOS) at a U.S. embassy or consulate outside of the United States, or an alien applying for admission at a U.S. port of entry.
The burden of proof to establish admissibility when seeking an immigration benefit is always on the alien. [34] The burden never shifts to USCIS at any time during adjudication. [35]

chunks.text:
The burden of proof to establish admissibility when seeking an immigration benefit is always on the alien. [34] The burden never shifts to USCIS at any time during adjudication. [35]
If there is evidence that would permit a reasonable person to conclude that the applicant has engaged in, is engaging in, or seeks to enter the United States to engage in, an offense described in 18 U.S.C. 1956 or 18 U.S.C. 1957 , or is or has been a knowing aider, abettor, assister, conspirator, or colluder with others in an offense described in 18 U.S.C. 1956 or 18 U.S.C. 1957 , then the applicant has not successfully met the burden of proof.
In these cases, USCIS considers the applicant inadmissible for having engaged in, engaging in, or seeking to enter the United States to engage in, an offense described in 18 U.S.C. 1956 or 18 U.S.C. 1957 , or being or having been a knowing aider, abettor, assister, conspirator, or colluder with others in an offense described in 18 U.S.C. 1956 or 18 U.S.C. 1957 , unless the applicant is able to successfully rebut the officer’s inadmissibility finding.
An alien who fails to meet the burden of proof is inadmissible under INA 212(a)(2)(I) unless the applicant is able to show clearly and beyond doubt [36] that he or she:
A finding of inadmissibility under INA 212(a)(2)(I) must be based on evidence, such as security and background checks, criminal convictions, arrest records, oral testimony, written testimony, or any other documentation containing information about the alien’s involvement in a money laundering offense described in 18 U.S.C. 1956 or 18 U.S.C. 1957 .
If the alien has been convicted under 18 U.S.C. 1956 or 18 U.S.C. 1957 , that conviction is evidence that the alien is inadmissible under INA 212(a)(2)(I) . However, a conviction is not required for an alien to be inadmissible under this ground.
USCIS considers responses on applications and petitions as evidence when determining if an alien is inadmissible under INA 212(a)(2)(I). [37] Some USCIS forms, including Form I-485 , require aliens to indicate if they have ever engaged in money laundering or have ever knowingly aided, assisted, abetted, conspired, or colluded with other in money laundering or seek to enter the United States to engage in such money laundering.
If an alien misrepresents information regarding money laundering when answering questions on Form I-485 , the alien could also be found inadmissible under INA 212(a)(6)(C)(i) . [38]
chunks.about: USCIS guidance to its officers: how the agency applies the regulations

chunks.citation: Volume 8, Part D, Chapter 15 - Money Laundering
chunks.heading: Chapter 15 - Money Laundering
chunks.text:
If an alien misrepresents information regarding money laundering when answering questions on Form I-485 , the alien could also be found inadmissible under INA 212(a)(6)(C)(i) . [38]
In general, USCIS is required to provide sufficient notice when derogatory information is uncovered during the course of the adjudication that is not known to the alien and USCIS intends to deny the benefit request on the basis of that derogatory information. [39] If the alien is unaware of the derogatory information and its impact on eligibility, USCIS must provide the alien an opportunity to rebut that information. [40]
The tables below map out the process for making money laundering admissibility determinations by class of aliens described in INA 212(a)(2)(I) .
The following table provides officers with an overview of how to determine whether an alien is inadmissible under INA 212(a)(2)(I)(i) . [41]
The officer may issue a Request for Evidence (RFE) or Notice of Intent to Deny (NOID) to the alien to provide him or her an opportunity to request a waiver, unless already requested.
If the waiver is approved, the alien may be admitted despite being inadmissible under INA 212(a)(2)(I). The officer should continue with the adjudication of the application.
An officer’s determination that an alien is inadmissible under INA 212(a)(2)(I)(i) should reflect facts demonstrating each of the factors in Steps 1 through 4 have been met.
When considering each of the factors in Steps 1 through 4, an officer should remember that the standard for his or her determination is that the officer “knows, or has reason to believe” that the alien “has engaged, is engaging, or seeks to enter the United States to engage” in money laundering. [45]
The following table provides officers with an overview of how to determine whether an alien is inadmissible as an aider, abettor, assister, conspirator, or colluder of an alien engaged in money laundering. [46]
The officer may issue an RFE or NOID to the alien to provide him or her an opportunity to request a waiver, unless already requested.
If the waiver is approved, the alien may be admitted despite being inadmissible under INA 212(a)(2)(I). The officer should continue with the adjudication of the application.
An officer only needs to determine that an alien has been a knowing aider, abettor, assister, conspirator, or colluder with money launderers. A conviction is not required for an alien to be inadmissible under this ground. However, if the alien was convicted of aiding, abetting, assisting, conspiring, or colluding with an alien engaged in money laundering, the conviction is evidence that the alien is inadmissible under INA 212(a)(2)(I)(ii) .

Some classifications of aliens may qualify for an exception or exemption from this ground of inadmissibility, and an inadmissibility determination is not required for those aliens. See Section G, Exceptions, Exemptions, and Waivers of Inadmissibility, Subsection 1, Exceptions [ 8 USCIS-PM D.15(G)(1) ], and Subsection 2, Exemptions [ 8 USCIS-PM D.15(G)(2) ].
[^ 47] See Section G, Exceptions, Exemptions, and Waivers of Inadmissibility, Subsection 3, Waivers [ 8 USCIS-PM D.15(G)(3) ].

chunks.citation: Volume 8, Part F, Chapter 3 - Immigrant Membership in Totalitarian Party
chunks.heading: Chapter 3 - Immigrant Membership in Totalitarian Party
chunks.text:
The inadmissibility ground for immigrant membership in or affiliation with the Communist or any other totalitarian party is part of a broader set of laws passed by Congress to address threats to the safety and security of the United States. Its original purpose was to protect the United States against un-American and subversive activities that were considered threats to national security.
In general, any immigrant who is or has been a member of or affiliated with the Communist or any other totalitarian party (or subdivision or affiliate), domestic or foreign, is inadmissible. [1] There are two exceptions to this ground of inadmissibility and a limited waiver available to certain aliens depending on the immigration benefit they are seeking. [2]
During and after World War I, the U.S. government was concerned with the external threats of anarchism and communism. In response, Congress passed the Immigration Act of 1918 that authorized the detention and deportation of alien anarchists under an extremely broad definition of anarchism irrespective of his or her date of entry into the United States. [3] Furthermore, Congress also criminalized the reentry of any alien who was previously deported under provisions of this Act. [4]
In 1938, Congress sought to protect the internal security, national defense, and foreign relations of the United States by requiring that foreigners disseminating propaganda and foreign ideologies be registered and identified. [5]
Near the onset of World War II, concern about the possibility of hostile foreign enemies living in the United States was on the rise. In response, Congress passed the Alien Registration Act of 1940. [6] With this Act, Congress made it a crime for any person to advocate for the overthrow or destruction of the U.S. government by force or violence, print or distribute materials advocating such activities, or organize any groups that advocate such activities. Congress also made it a crime for any person to attempt or conspire to commit such acts. The Act also established a removal ground for aliens convicted of these new offenses within 5 years of entry or convicted more than once at any time after entry. [7]
In the aftermath of World War II and in response to the rise of communism in the global arena, Congress passed a succession of laws, including the Internal Security Act of 1950. [8] Through the Internal Security Act of 1950, Congress aimed to combat the world communism movement and prosecute those who knowingly and willfully participated. [9]

chunks.citation: Volume 8, Part F, Chapter 3 - Immigrant Membership in Totalitarian Party
chunks.heading: Chapter 3 - Immigrant Membership in Totalitarian Party
chunks.text:
The Internal Security Act of 1950 created criminal penalties for conspiring to create a totalitarian dictatorship in the United States and to unlawfully communicate or receive classified information. It did not create criminal penalties for membership or the holding of office in a communist organization, but required communist organizations to register, submit annual reports, and prohibited the members of communist organizations from applying for, renewing, or using a U.S. passport. [10]
The Internal Security Act of 1950 also amended the Immigration Act of 1918 by adding new grounds of exclusion specific to members of communist or totalitarian parties, affiliates of such groups, or to aliens who advocate the doctrines of world communism or any other form of totalitarianism. [11] It likewise expanded the deportation provisions to cover such aliens.
The Act also created new restrictions on naturalization by making aliens who were members or affiliates of a communist organization or who advocated certain communist or totalitarian positions (or were members or affiliates of organizations that advocated such positions) ineligible for naturalization. [12] Naturalized citizens who engaged in such activities within 5 years following their naturalization would be subject to revocation of their naturalization orders.
A year later, Congress amended the Internal Security Act of 1950 to include some of the exceptions to the grounds of exclusion specific to the members and affiliates of communist organizations to better align the actual language of the statute with the intent of Congress. The amendment stated that only membership or affiliation which was voluntary would be considered for exclusion and would not include membership or affiliation which is or was solely when the alien was under 16 years of age, by operation of law, or for purposes of obtaining employment, food rations, or other essentials of living and where necessary for such purposes. [13]
Subsequently, Congress passed the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) of 1952 which, for the first time, authorized the exclusion of all aliens, immigrants or nonimmigrants, on the basis of membership in or affiliation with the Communist or any other totalitarian party. [14] As with previous acts, the INA of 1952 also declared that aliens were excludable based on a wide variety of other activities linked to the Communist Party or other totalitarian parties even if the aliens were not members or affiliates.

chunks.citation: Volume 8, Part F, Chapter 3 - Immigrant Membership in Totalitarian Party
chunks.heading: Chapter 3 - Immigrant Membership in Totalitarian Party
chunks.text:
The INA of 1952 included exceptions and waivers similar to those available today. There were two classes of exceptions available to immigrants and nonimmigrants alike. The first, which was based solely on the alien's personal history (and tracked the Internal Security Act amendments of 1951), excepted aliens if their membership or affiliation “is or was involuntary, or is or was solely when under sixteen years of age, by operation of law, or for purposes of obtaining employment, food rations, or other essentials of living and where necessary for such purposes.” [15]
The second exception was available to aliens whose admission “would be in the public interest” if their membership or affiliation had terminated at least 5 years before the date of the application and the alien had been “actively opposed to the doctrine, program, principles, and ideology” of the Communist or totalitarian organization during those 5 years. [16]
The INA of 1952 also contained an exception for nonimmigrant diplomats (A) and nonimmigrant representatives of international organizations (G) as well as a general waiver for temporary admission as a nonimmigrant. [17] The general waiver for aliens seeking nonimmigrant visas was only to be granted in the discretion of the Attorney General based on the recommendation of the Secretary of State or a consular officer.
Subsequent amendments provided for additional exceptions. In 1977, Congress passed the Foreign Relations Authorization Act of Fiscal Year 1978, which contained a provision popularly referred to as the “McGovern Amendment.” [18] This provision slightly modified the operation of the nonimmigrant waiver established in INA 212(d)(3). While the INA stated that an excludable alien applying for a nonimmigrant visa would only receive the visa and be admitted in the discretion of the Attorney General based on a recommendation by the Secretary of State or a consular officer, the McGovern Amendment required the Secretary of State to make a favorable recommendation to the Attorney General within 30 days of receiving the nonimmigrant visa application unless “the admission of such alien would be contrary to the security interests of the United States.” [19]
Congress limited the scope of the McGovern Amendment in 1979 with a provision in the Department of State Authorization Act, Fiscal Years 1980 and 1981, by eliminating eligibility for the McGovern Amendment for three groups: representatives of “purported labor organizations” that were actually instruments of totalitarian states; members, officers, officials, representatives, and spokesmen of the Palestine Liberation Organization; and aliens from countries that signed the Helsinki Final Act but which were not in substantial compliance with its provisions. [20]

chunks.citation: Volume 8, Part F, Chapter 3 - Immigrant Membership in Totalitarian Party
chunks.heading: Chapter 3 - Immigrant Membership in Totalitarian Party
chunks.text:
The Immigration Act of 1990 (IMMACT 90) com pletely reorganized the exclusion grounds, amending some and deleting others. [21] While Congress retained the exclusion ground in the INA relating to membership or affiliation, with IMMACT 90, Congress eliminated the various other related exclusion grounds such as those that penalized the advocacy or publication of communist or other subversive views or materials.
The IMMACT 90 exclusion provision related to membership in the Communist or other totalitarian party is nearly identical to the current inadmissibility ground at INA 212(a)(3)(D), with two minor differences. [22] Through IMMACT 90, Congress limited the exclusion ground to “immigrants” rather than applying this provision on its own terms to “aliens” more generally. [23] While nonimmigrant members of communist or totalitarian parties cannot be found inadmissible based on INA 212(a)(3)(D), they may be found inadmissible based on other grounds, if applicable.
The naturalization provisions contain a separate but related ineligibility ground for an alien who has been a member of (or affiliated with) the Communist or any other totalitarian party within 10 years of filing and until the applicant takes the Oath of Allegiance. [24] As in the inadmissibility context, there are statutory exceptions to the naturalization bar based on past membership and past involuntary membership. [25] The regulations related to naturalization contain definitions and concepts concerning the Communist Party or other totalitarian parties that USCIS also applies to its interpretation of the inadmissibility ground found at INA 212(a)(3)(D). [26]
In general, any immigrant who is or has been a member of or affiliated with the Communist or any other totalitarian party (or subdivision or affiliate thereof), domestic or foreign, is inadmissible. [27]
This ground of inadmissibility applies to an alien seeking immigrant status, such as an applicant inside the United States applying for adjustment of status to that of a lawful permanent resident (LPR), an applicant for an immigrant visa with the U.S. Department of State (DOS) at a U.S. embassy or consulate outside of the United States, or an applicant for admission as an immigrant at a U.S. port of entry. [28]
The inadmissibility ground applies to membership (past or present) and those with an affiliation with such parties. There are certain exceptions to this ground of inadmissibility as well as a waiver. [29]
The following table provides officers with an overview of how to determine whether an applicant is inadmissible under INA 212(a)(3)(D) .
An immigrant who is or has been a member of or affiliated with the Communist or any other totalitarian party is inadmissible under INA 212(a)(3)(D), unless an exception applies.

chunks.citation: Volume 8, Part F, Chapter 3 - Immigrant Membership in Totalitarian Party
chunks.heading: Chapter 3 - Immigrant Membership in Totalitarian Party
chunks.text:
The following table provides officers with an overview of how to determine whether an applicant is inadmissible under INA 212(a)(3)(D) .
An immigrant who is or has been a member of or affiliated with the Communist or any other totalitarian party is inadmissible under INA 212(a)(3)(D), unless an exception applies.
Under INA 212(a)(3)(D), an officer must first determine whether the organization in question meets the definition of Communist or any other totalitarian party.
The regulations define the Communist Party as:
“Any other totalitarian party” is defined as “an organization which advocates the establishment in the United States of a totalitarian dictatorship or totalitarianism.” [31]
“Totalitarian dictatorship” or “totalitarianism” refer to systems of government not representative in fact, characterized by:
After determining that the group in question meets the definition of the Communist or any other totalitarian party, the officer must determine if the person is or has been a member of or affiliated with that group. If the group does not meet the definition, then the person is not inadmissible under this ground.
Membership
Membership may be established by the applicant’s testimony alone, where that testimony shows a sufficiently viable and purposeful relationship. [33] Membership is not defined in the INA or in the regulations, and is dependent on a person satisfying the requirements for membership as specified by the membership organization in question.
Membership may be established by evidence that the applicant was issued a membership card, paid dues to the organization, [34] or even based on witness testimony regarding the applicant’s membership in the organization (including seeing the applicant’s name on membership records, dues records, and testimony regarding meeting attendance). [35]
Affiliation
Even if an immigrant is not a member of the Communist or any other totalitarian party, he or she may still be inadmissible if found to be an affiliate of such an organization. The INA states that while “the giving, loaning, or promising of support or of money or any other thing of value for any other purpose to any organization shall be presumed to constitute affiliation . . . nothing in this paragraph shall be construed as an exclusive definition of affiliation.” [36]
Affiliation implies less than membership but more than sympathy. [37] Affiliation includes more than mere interest or sympathy for an organization but may also be accompanied by some positive and voluntary action that provides support, money, or another thing of value. [38] The regulations state that “[a]ffiliation with an organization includes, but is not limited to, the giving, lending, or promising of support or of money or anything of value, to that organization to be used for any purpose.” [39]

chunks.citation: Volume 8, Part F, Chapter 3 - Immigrant Membership in Totalitarian Party
chunks.heading: Chapter 3 - Immigrant Membership in Totalitarian Party
chunks.text:
“Affiliate” is also used in the context of this inadmissibility ground to describe links between organizations, in addition to ties between a person and an organization. An affiliate organization of a totalitarian party is one that is related to, or identified with, a proscribed association or party [40] in such close association as to evidence an adherence to or a furtherance of the purposes and objectives of such association or party, or as to indicate a working alliance to bring to fruition the purposes and objectives of the proscribed association or party. [41]
Special Considerations for Military and Government Service
Service in the armed forces of a communist or totalitarian-controlled country, whether voluntary or not, does not in itself constitute or establish applicant’s membership in or affiliation with a communist or totalitarian party. [42] Notwithstanding, if the applicant’s service in the armed forces is inherently political, the applicant is inadmissible as a member or affiliate of a communist or totalitarian party. In such cases, the officer should determine if the evidence supports a finding that the applicant was aware of the political nature of his or her military service. For example, an applicant may occupy a sufficiently high rank in the armed forces of his or her country that is inherently political or perform a specific mission that is inherently political.
If the applicant was or is a government worker in a communist or communist-controlled country, then the officer should give special attention and scrutinize such employment since voluntary service in a political capacity constitutes affiliation with a political party or the organization in power at the time of service. [43]
Even if the officer has determined that the applicant is or has been a member of or affiliate of a proscribed group, the evidence must show that the applicant’s membership or affiliation was meaningful when finding the applicant inadmissible.
“Meaningful” membership or affiliation versus “non-meaningful” membership or affiliation has never been codified in the INA but is rather a judicially created concept. In general, membership in a communist or totalitarian party must be intentional in order to be meaningful. Most notably, the Supreme Court of the United States has held that “[t]here must be a substantial basis for finding that an alien committed himself to the Communist Party in consciousness that he was ‘joining an organization known as the Communist Party which operates as a distinct and active political organization[.]’” [44]
chunks.about: USCIS guidance to its officers: how the agency applies the regulations

chunks.citation: Volume 8, Part F, Chapter 3 - Immigrant Membership in Totalitarian Party
chunks.heading: Chapter 3 - Immigrant Membership in Totalitarian Party
chunks.text:
An alien’s membership or affiliation is meaningful if the evidence shows that the alien is aware of the political aspects of the proscribed organization during the time of their membership or if the evidence shows that the alien engaged in party activities to a degree that substantially supports an inference of his or her awareness of the party’s political aspect. [45] Accordingly, an alien's knowledge or awareness of a communist or totalitarian party’s political nature is sufficient to establish that an alien’s membership is meaningful. [46]
A finding of inadmissibility under INA 212(a)(3)(D) must be based on evidence, such as oral testimony, written testimony, or any other documentation containing information about the applicant’s current or prior membership in or affiliation with the Communist or any other totalitarian party. Some USCIS forms, including the Application to Register Permanent Residence or Adjust Status ( Form I-485 ), require applicants to list their memberships in organizations and parties.
Membership or affiliation is a question of fact for the officer to determine. If the facts and evidence available would allow a reasonable person to conclude that the applicant is a member or an affiliate of the Communist or any other totalitarian party, then the applicant must establish that he or she qualifies for one of the exceptions or the waiver.
If an applicant misrepresents information regarding membership or affiliation in answering questions on Form I-485, the applicant could also be found inadmissible under INA 212(a)(6)(C)(i). [47]
The burden of proof to establish admissibility when seeking an immigration benefit is always on the applicant. [48] The burden never shifts to the Government at any time during adjudication. [49]
To determine whether an applicant is inadmissible based on his or her membership in or affiliation with the Communist or any other totalitarian party, there must be sufficient evidence that would lead a reasonable person to find that he or she is or was a member of or affiliated with a proscribed group. [50] If there is evidence that would permit a reasonable person to conclude that the applicant is inadmissible under this ground, then the officer should find that the applicant has not successfully met the burden of proof. If there is any adverse, third-party information in the record, then the officer conducting an interview is generally expected to confront the applicant with the information and resolve the issue at the time of the interview.

chunks.citation: Volume 8, Part F, Chapter 3 - Immigrant Membership in Totalitarian Party
chunks.heading: Chapter 3 - Immigrant Membership in Totalitarian Party
chunks.text:
If an officer is basing a decision in whole or in part on information of which the applicant is unaware or could not reasonably be expected to be aware, and the applicant was not confronted with that information and given an opportunity to respond during an interview, the officer must issue a Notice of Intent to Deny (NOID). [51] The NOID provides the applicant an opportunity to review and respond to the information, unless the information is classified. [52] An applicant who fails to meet the burden of proof is inadmissible for being a member or affiliate of the Communist or any other totalitarian party, unless the applicant is able to successfully rebut the officer’s inadmissibility finding. [53]
If the applicant is successful in rebutting the inadmissibility finding, the officer should find that the applicant is not inadmissible for being a member or affiliate of the Communist or any other totalitarian party.
Congress provided two statutory exceptions for immigrants who might otherwise be found inadmissible for their membership in or affiliation with the Communist or any other totalitarian party. There are two categories of exceptions: involuntary membership and past membership.
Involuntary Membership
The first category of exceptions applies to immigrants whose membership or affiliation is or was:
Membership or affiliation is considered involuntary when it is the result of factors such as coercion, fraud, duress, incapacity, or some other error which may impair or negate the capacity for affirmative and intentional actions. [55] The burden remains on the applicant to establish that the association is involuntary. [56]
An exception also applies when such membership or affiliation occurred solely when the applicant was under the age of 16. [57] However, political activities and continuing commitments after the age of 16 are not protected under this exception. [58]
The statute also excepts membership or affiliation occurring solely by operation of law. This includes any case where “the alien automatically, and without personal acquiescence, became a member of or affiliated with a proscribed party or organization by official act, proclamation, order, edict, or decree.” [59]
Joining a proscribed organization in order to obtain the essentials of living is also excepted, absent an ideological commitment to the cause. [60] Examples of the essentials of living refer to “food, shelter, clothing, employment and an education which were routinely available to the rest of the population.” [61]
chunks.about: USCIS guidance to its officers: how the agency applies the regulations

chunks.citation: Volume 8, Part F, Chapter 3 - Immigrant Membership in Totalitarian Party
chunks.heading: Chapter 3 - Immigrant Membership in Totalitarian Party
chunks.text:
Joining a proscribed organization in order to obtain the essentials of living is also excepted, absent an ideological commitment to the cause. [60] Examples of the essentials of living refer to “food, shelter, clothing, employment and an education which were routinely available to the rest of the population.” [61]
Under the INA, an immigrant is not inadmissible when his membership in or affiliation with a communist or totalitarian party is necessary in order to obtain food or employment. Inadmissibility “shall not apply to an alien because of membership or affiliation if the alien establishes . . . that the membership or affiliation is or was . . . for purposes of obtaining employment, food rations, or other essentials of living and whether necessary for such purposes.” [62] If the immigrant’s membership or affiliation with a communist or totalitarian party was not actually necessary for purposes of such essentials of living, then the immigrant is inadmissible unless another exception applies.
Past Membership
If an officer has determined that the applicant has been a member of or affiliated with a proscribed organization and one of the involuntary membership exceptions does not apply, the officer should evaluate whether the past membership exception applies to the applicant.
An immigrant may be excepted from inadmissibility under INA 212(a)(3)(D) if the immigrant can establish that:
In cases that involve past membership, mere termination for the requisite time period is sufficient; active opposition is not required. [65] It is also the applicant’s burden to prove that he or she is not a threat to the security of United States.
Furthermore, where the evidence shows that the immigrant is a threat to the security of the United States, the immigrant may also be inadmissible under security and related grounds [66] or terrorist activities. [67] An immigrant may be found to be a threat to the security of the United States and ineligible for the exception even if not inadmissible under a separate security or terrorist inadmissibility ground. [68]
If the officer finds that a meaningful membership or affiliation in a proscribed organization exists, and the immigrant does not qualify for either of the two exceptions, then the officer should find the immigrant inadmissible under INA 212(a)(3)(D) for being or having been a member of the Communist or any other totalitarian party.
